title: The København
subtitle: København · South Atlantic, 1928
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.
grade: Desaturated documentary still, the open South Atlantic in the southern summer of 1928, late age of sail, slate-blue and grey-green water under pale high light, cold and melancholy and uncanny, period maritime detail, cinematic vertical composition, fine film grain. Single image, not a collage, no text, no signage, no flags, no people, no faces.

beats.vo: The South Atlantic, December nineteen twenty-eight. The København, then the largest sailing ship in the world, left Buenos Aires for Australia.
beats.img: A huge steel five-masted barque under full sail, dark hull, tall masts carrying tiers of pale square sails, seen broadside and centred in the middle third of a vertical frame on a deep blue-grey open sea in bright clear daylight, every mast and sail sharply legible, white water at the bow, no flags, no lettering on the hull, no people.

beats.vo: Sixty people were aboard. Forty-five were cadets, most of them teenagers.
beats.img: The empty cadets' quarters below deck on a 1920s sailing ship, two rows of narrow wooden bunks with neatly folded grey wool blankets, small wooden sea chests at their feet, a shaft of soft daylight falling from a deck skylight onto the centre of the floor, vertical composition, still and deserted, no people.

beats.vo: Eight days out, she radioed a passing steamer that all was well. When it called her again, she did not answer.
beats.img: A small 1920s ship's wireless room at night, a black-panelled radio telegraph set with softly glowing valves and brass dials centred on a wooden desk, a telegraph key and a pair of headphones resting beside it, a single shaded lamp, an empty chair pushed back, vertical composition, no people, no legible text.

beats.vo: A search across the South Atlantic lasted months. Reported sightings followed. None was ever confirmed.
beats.img: A small 1920s steamship centred far out on a vast grey South Atlantic sea, tiny against long rolling swells under a low pale overcast sky, a thin trail of smoke from her funnel, the horizon around her completely empty, vertical frame, no people.

beats.vo: No one aboard was ever seen again. Nearly a century later, no wreck has ever been confirmed.
beats.img: A wide empty open ocean in late-afternoon light in a vertical frame, long blue-grey swells rolling toward a pale bright band on the horizon, nothing on the water anywhere, vast, silent and unresolved.

facts.claim: København: Danish five-masted barque, built 1921 by Ramage & Ferguson, Leith, for the East Asiatic Company as a cargo-carrying training ship; at the time the largest sailing ship in the world (yearbook: 'den daværende verdens største sejlskib')

Final voyage: reached Buenos Aires 17 Nov 1928; sailed in ballast 14 Dec 1928 bound for Australia (Adelaide per the Danish maritime museum yearbook and lex.dk; Melbourne per one secondary source, so the film says only 'Australia')

60 people aboard, 45 of them cadets ('elever'); cadets aged about 15-20. NOTE: English Wikipedia gives 75 (26 crew + 45 cadets); the Danish maritime museum yearbook (Handels- og Søfartsmuseet), lex.dk and the Copenhagen Post all give 60, which we use. 45 cadets is consistent across every source

Last contact: radio exchange with the Norwegian steamer William Blumer, 21-22 Dec 1928 (eight days out); she reported all was well (yearbook: the wind had risen and she was making 11 knots). When the Blumer tried again the following night there was no reply

Search: the East Asiatic Company's motor ship Mexico (from May 1929) plus chartered ships and British naval help searched the South Atlantic for months; called off early September 1929 with nothing found. A maritime inquiry (søforhør, set for 15 Oct 1929) closed the case legally; no source states it established a cause, so the film names no finding

Reported sightings (Tristan da Cunha, 21 Jan 1929; a 'phantom ship' reported by an Argentine crew 1930; others) were never confirmed; the Tristan sighting was later attributed to the four-masted barque Ponape / a Finnish ship. Used only as 'reported sightings', never as fact

No one aboard was ever seen again; no wreck has ever been confirmed. Reported finds (stern piece off Western Australia, 1935 remains in SW Africa, a 1934 bottle message later shown copied from a novel, an unidentified wreck and 'O'/'D' letters at Tristan da Cunha) have never been confirmed as the København. Ingeniøren Dec 2025: 'man har aldrig fundet den mindste rest af skibet'; Ingeniøren June 2026: divers and researchers have not been able to establish with certainty where she ended
